content: The publication by Purcell JE, Uye S, and Lo W-T (2007) explores the anthropogenic causes of jellyfish blooms and their direct consequences for humans. This review, published in Marine Ecology Progress Series, highlights the significant impact of human activities on jellyfish population dynamics and the resulting implications for human health and ecosystems. Quail MT (2019) discusses the hazards associated with warm water environments, specifically focusing on sea lice and seabather’s eruption. This article, published in Nursing, provides insights into the clinical presentation and management of these conditions. Rayon-Viñá F, Miralles L, Gómez-Agenjo M, Dopico E, and Garcia-Vazquez E (2018) examine marine litter in the South Bay of Biscay. Their study, published in Marine Pollution Bulletin, identifies local differences in beach littering and links these variations to citizen perceptions and awareness, emphasizing the role of public engagement in addressing marine pollution. Remigante A, Costa R, Morabito R, La Spada G, Marino A, and Dossena S (2018) investigate the impact of scyphozoan jellyfish venoms on human health and evaluate current first aid options for jellyfish stings. Their findings, published in Toxins, provide evidence-based recommendations for managing jellyfish envenomations. Scanlan CM, Foden J, Wells E, and Best MA (2007) discuss the monitoring of opportunistic macroalgal blooms in the context of the Water Framework Directive. Schneider TJ, Maguire GS, Whisson DA, and Weston MA (2019) highlight the failure of regulations to effectively limit dog activity in beach habitats critical to threatened species. Staggs R and Pay JL (2019) provide an overview of cnidarian toxicity, detailing the mechanisms and effects of venom from jellyfish and related species. This resource, available through the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI), serves as a comprehensive guide for understanding cnidarian envenomations. Suthanthangjai M, Moore K, Steel G, and Hughey K (2013) compare two survey approaches to track environmental perceptions among New Zealanders. Published in the International Journal of Science and Society, this study offers insights into public attitudes toward environmental issues and the effectiveness of different survey methodologies. Tudor DT and Williams AT (2006) analyze the factors influencing public beach selection along the coast of Wales, UK. Their research, published in Area, identifies key criteria that drive beachgoer preferences, providing valuable information for coastal management and tourism planning. The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) (2009) addresses the global challenge of marine litter in a report published in Nairobi, Kenya. This document emphasizes the need for international cooperation and policy interventions to mitigate the environmental and economic impacts of marine debris. Ward NT, Darracq MA, Tomaszewski C, and Clark RF (2012) present evidence-based treatment strategies for jellyfish stings in North America and Hawaii. Published in Annals of Emergency Medicine, their work provides practical guidelines for healthcare providers managing jellyfish envenomations. White M, Pahl S, Wheeler B, Fleming L, and Depledge M (2016) explore the concept of the Blue Gym, examining the health and well-being benefits of engaging with blue spaces such as oceans and lakes. Their study, published in the Journal of the Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom, also highlights the reciprocal responsibility of individuals to protect these environments. Widmer WM and Reis RA (2010) evaluate the effectiveness of beach ashtrays in reducing marine contamination. Their experimental study, published in the Brazilian Archives of Biology and Technology, demonstrates the potential of simple interventions to mitigate littering on beaches. Williams AT, Randerson P, Di Giacomo C, Anfuso G, Macias A, and Perales JA (2016) investigate the distribution of beach litter along the coastline of Cádiz, Spain. Published in Marine Pollution Bulletin, their findings provide a detailed analysis of litter patterns and their environmental implications. Winton DJ, Anderson LG, Rocliffe S, and Loiselle S (2020) focus on macroplastic pollution in freshwater environments, emphasizing the need for public and policy action. Their study, published in Science of the Total Environment, highlights the growing threat of plastic pollution and the importance of targeted interventions. Wyles KJ, Pahl S, Holland M, and Thompson RC (2017) compare the outcomes of beach clean-up activities with other coastal engagement initiatives. Published in Environment and Behavior, their research suggests that beach cleans can have broader environmental and social benefits beyond litter removal. Zielinski S, Botero CM, and Yanes A (2019) critically review beach cleaning methods and their environmental impacts. Their work, published in Marine Pollution Bulletin, provides a comprehensive evaluation of the effectiveness and sustainability of various cleaning approaches. Zimmer J-Y, Haubruge E, and Francis F (2014) synthesize research on the larval ecology of biting midges (Diptera: Ceratopogonidae). Published in Biotechnology, Agronomy, and Society, this French-language review offers insights into the ecological dynamics of these insects. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for recreational water quality aim to protect public health by ensuring the safe management of coastal, estuarine, and freshwater environments. These guidelines describe the potential adverse health impacts of recreational water use, recommend national health-based targets, and outline systems for monitoring and controlling risks. They also emphasize the health and well-being benefits of recreational water use, including relaxation, exercise, and cultural practices, while highlighting the economic advantages for local and national economies. The guidelines are intended for national and local authorities and other entities responsible for ensuring the safety of recreational water sites.
